questions.statement: Complete the sentence with the correct comparative: 'Lima is ___ than Cusco.'
questions.context: A student compares two cities.

options.text: bigger
options.feedback: Correct. A comparative adjective takes the -er ending, and 'than' is supplied by the second part of the sentence.

options.text: the biggest
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The biggest' is a superlative, which compares three or more items rather than two.

options.text: bigger than is
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Bigger than is' misplaces the comparative and adds an extra verb.

options.text: big
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Big' is the base form and cannot express a comparison on its own.

questions.explanation:
Comparative forms compare two items and are normally followed by than, whereas superlatives compare at least three.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct superlative of the adjective 'good'.
questions.context: A traveller compares three routes.

options.text: the better
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The better' is a comparative form and compares only two items.

options.text: the best
options.feedback: Correct. Good has an irregular superlative, 'the best', formed by adding the definite article.

options.text: the goodest
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The goodest' does not exist; good is irregular.

options.text: more good
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More good' misapplies the pattern used with longer adjectives such as 'more expensive'.

questions.explanation:
The three adjectives good, bad and far are irregular in both the comparative and the superlative.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct comparative of 'expensive'.
questions.context: An essay compares two similar options using a longer adjective.

options.text: most expensive
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Most expensive' is the superlative, which compares three or more items.

options.text: expensiver
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Expensiver' adds the -er ending, which is only correct for short adjectives.

options.text: more expensive
options.feedback: Correct. Longer adjectives form the comparative with 'more' plus the base form.

options.text: more expensive than is
options.feedback: Wrong. The extra 'than is' makes the phrase ungrammatical when compared is already implied by the sentence.

questions.explanation:
Adjectives of more than one syllable normally take more and most rather than the -er and -est endings.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence expressing equality between two things.
questions.context: A classmate compares two amounts that are the same.

options.text: My bag is heavier like yours.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Heavier like' has no grammatical basis in English comparison.

options.text: My bag is more heavy than yours.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More heavy' uses the wrong form, and 'than' expresses inequality rather than equality.

options.text: My bag is so heavy as yours.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'So plus adjective plus as' is not a valid construction in standard English.

options.text: My bag is as heavy as yours.
options.feedback: Correct. 'As plus adjective plus as' expresses that two things are equal in that quality.

questions.explanation:
Equality is expressed with as plus adjective plus as, and this pattern is the counterpart of the comparative with than.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct comparative sentence about speed.
questions.context: An ad compares two broadband plans.

options.text: This plan is twice as fast as the other one.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Twice as' plus adjective plus 'as' expresses exactly double the comparative quality.

options.text: This plan is twice as fastest as the other one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Fastest' is a superlative and cannot be used in a two-way comparison.

options.text: This plan is twice as faster as the other one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Faster' is a comparative form and cannot follow 'as'.

options.text: This plan is twice as fast than the other one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'As' already carries the comparison, so adding 'than' produces a mixed construction.

questions.explanation:
When a ratio such as twice or three times is used, the pattern is as plus adjective plus as, without any comparative or superlative ending.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct sentence comparing two distances.
questions.context: A grammar task tests comparative forms of irregular adjectives.

options.text: The trail is further than the road.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Further' is used mainly in the sense of additional quantity or advancement rather than physical distance.

options.text: The trail is farther than the road.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Far' takes the ending -er in this form, giving 'farther' for physical distance.

options.text: The trail is the farther than the road.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The farther' is not a valid comparative construction in English.

options.text: The trail is farer than the road.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Farer' is not a standard form of the word.

questions.explanation:
Far has two comparative forms with different meanings: farther for physical distance and further for additional quantity or advancement.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly intensifies a comparative.
questions.context: A study explains degree in comparison.

options.text: This route is longest than the other one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Longest' is a superlative and cannot be followed by 'than'.

options.text: This route is more longer than the other one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More' cannot be added to a short adjective that already takes the -er ending.

options.text: This route is much longer than the other one.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Much' intensifies an already comparative form without any change to the adjective itself.

options.text: This route is much more long than the other one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More long' misuses the pattern for long adjectives with a short adjective that takes -er.

questions.explanation:
Intensifiers such as much, far, a lot and considerably modify the comparative form, and they never trigger the 'more' pattern.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct superlative sentence.
questions.context: A report compares consumption figures across three countries.

options.text: Peru consumes lesser tea than any of the three countries.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Lesser' is not used with uncountable nouns such as tea.

options.text: Peru consumes less tea than any of the three countries is true.
options.feedback: Wrong. The clause cannot be completed with 'is true' because the structure already contains the comparison.

options.text: Peru consumes the least tea of any of the three countries.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Less' is a comparative form and cannot compare three countries at once.

options.text: Peru consumes less tea than any of the three countries.
options.feedback: Correct. 'The least' is the superlative of the little family and is required when comparing three or more items.

questions.explanation:
With three or more items a superlative is needed, and for little the correct form is the least rather than less.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence expressing a comparison that is becoming progressively true.
questions.context: A speaker compares a developing situation with an earlier state.

options.text: The city is getting more crowded every year.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Getting' plus a comparative expresses a gradual increase, which is the standard pattern for this trend.

options.text: The city is getting as more crowded every year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'As more' mixes the equality pattern with a comparative, which is not a valid combination.

options.text: The city is getting most crowded every year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Most crowded' is a superlative and cannot describe an ongoing increase.

options.text: The city is getting more crowdeder every year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Crowdeder' is not a valid form; crowded is a short adjective that takes -er.

questions.explanation:
The construction getting plus comparative is the usual way English describes a continuing change rather than a fixed comparison.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct sentence comparing the frequency of two actions.
questions.context: An exam tests comparative adverbs.

options.text: She goes to the library more frequently than her brother.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More often' mixes the adverbial case of 'often' with the comparative pattern used for adverbs ending in -ly.

options.text: She goes to the library more often than her brother.
options.feedback: Correct. 'More frequently' is the comparative of the adverb 'frequently' and needs the -ly form plus more.

options.text: She goes to the library most often than her brother.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Most often' is a superlative and cannot be followed by 'than'.

options.text: She goes to the library often more than her brother.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Often more than' misplaces the comparative phrase and breaks the normal word order.

questions.explanation:
Short adverbs such as often and fast often take the -er ending, while adverbs ending in -ly normally take more before them.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence with the correct comparative of 'fast'.
questions.context: A speaker compares two people using a short adverb.

options.text: He runs fastest than I do.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Fastest' is a superlative and cannot be followed by 'than'.

options.text: He runs more fast than I do.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More fast' is not used because fast is a short adverb that takes -er.

options.text: He runs faster than I do.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Fast' takes the -er ending in the comparative, so 'faster' is correct before 'than'.

options.text: He runs as fast than I do.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'As' introduces equality or a condition, so it cannot be combined with 'than'.

questions.explanation:
Adverbs such as fast, hard, late and early take the -er ending just as their corresponding adjectives do.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the statement that explains why 'more easier' is incorrect.
questions.context: A grammarian explains a common error.

options.text: 'Easier' is a superlative and cannot be compared.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Easier' is a comparative, not a superlative, so the explanation is wrong.

options.text: 'More' can only be used with uncountable nouns, which is why it fails here.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More' is not restricted to uncountable nouns; it modifies longer adjectives and adverbs.

options.text: 'Easy' is a long adjective and therefore requires 'more' in the comparative.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Easy' is a short adjective and does not require 'more'.

options.text: 'Easy' already takes the -er ending, so adding 'more' doubles the comparative and is ungrammatical.
options.feedback: Correct. This identifies the exact mechanism of the error, since easy forms its comparative with -er rather than with more.

questions.explanation:
Explaining an error accurately means identifying which inflection pattern the adjective follows, not generalising about word length.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly expresses a decline.
questions.context: An exam tests a comparison with a decreasing quantity.

options.text: Attendance has dropped considerably since the new timetable.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Considerably' intensifies the past participle 'dropped' to show the size of the decline.

options.text: Attendance has dropped considerably more since the new timetable.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Considerably more' would leave 'more' with nothing to modify, since the degree is already stated.

options.text: Attendance has drop considerably since the new timetable.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Drop' is the base form and lacks the participle needed after 'has'.

options.text: Attendance has dropped more considerably since the new timetable.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More considerably' treats the participle as if it took the 'more' comparative pattern, which it does not.

questions.explanation:
Intensifying a past participle in a perfect construction takes an adverb such as considerably, without any comparative ending.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence expressing two quantities changing equally.
questions.context: A speaker compares two quantities that have increased at the same rate.

options.text: Prices rose more steeply than wages last year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More steeply than' would express a difference in degree, which contradicts the point being made.

options.text: Prices rose as steeply as wages last year.
options.feedback: Correct. 'As steeply as' states that the two quantities rose by the same degree.

options.text: Prices rose the steeply than wages last year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The steeply than' is not a valid construction.

options.text: Prices rose as more steeply as wages last year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'As more steeply as' mixes the equality and comparative patterns in one phrase.

questions.explanation:
Equality of degree with an adverb is expressed with as plus the adverb plus as, in the same way as adjectives.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly expresses that one option is not better than another.
questions.context: A grammar task tests the negative comparative.

options.text: The train is no more expensive than the bus.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Not more expensive than' is grammatically possible but the preferred form in careful writing is 'no more'.

options.text: The train is not more expensive than the bus is.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Not more' is understood but is less idiomatic than 'no more' in formal English.

options.text: The train is not more expensive than the bus.
options.feedback: Correct. 'No more' is the idiomatic negative comparative and states that no additional cost is involved.

options.text: The train is not most expensive than the bus.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Not most' uses a superlative in a two-way comparison, which is wrong.

questions.explanation:
English has an idiomatic negative comparative, no plus comparative, which is preferred over the plainer not plus comparative.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the explanation that accounts for the use of 'the' in 'the fastest car in the class'.
questions.context: A language learner asks about an apparently inconsistent comparison.

options.text: The article is optional here and the sentence is equally natural without it.
options.feedback: Wrong. Omitting the article in a superlative would normally be marked as incorrect in an examination.

options.text: The article is required because the sentence uses the word 'in' rather than 'than'.
options.feedback: Wrong. The preposition plays no role in whether the superlative takes an article.

options.text: The article is required because 'fast' is an irregular adjective.
options.feedback: Wrong. Fast is entirely regular and its article has nothing to do with irregularity.

options.text: Superlatives normally take the definite article because they pick out a unique item from a set.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the standard account of the definite article with superlatives, which identify a single outstanding item.

questions.explanation:
The article with superlatives is a grammatical pattern in its own right, and it must be justified in terms of uniqueness rather than accident.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence conveys the comparison with the greatest precision?
questions.context: A writing task asks the learner to choose the most precise comparison.

options.text: The new route is nearly three times shorter than the old one.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Nearly three times shorter' combines a precise ratio with a hedge and is idiomatic in careful English.

options.text: The new route is the most short of the old one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The most short' is not a valid superlative and 'of' follows the wrong noun.

options.text: The new route is very short than the old one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Very short than' mixes an intensifier with a comparative that is not present.

options.text: The new route is three times more short than the old one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Three times more short' double-marks the comparison and is not a standard construction.

questions.explanation:
Precision in comparison comes from combining an accurate ratio with an appropriate hedge such as nearly or almost.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly states that two things are of equal size.
questions.context: An exam tests a comparison where the subject and the compared item are equal.

options.text: The two rooms are the same sizer.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Sizer' is not an English noun and cannot express this comparison.

options.text: The two rooms are the same size.
options.feedback: Correct. 'The same size' is the standard nominal comparison used to state that two things match in that quality.

options.text: The two rooms are as same size.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'As same' mixes the equality pattern with the adjective same, which is redundant and wrong.

options.text: The two rooms are same size.
options.feedback: Wrong. The article is required before 'same' in this construction.

questions.explanation:
The same plus noun is one of the commonest nominal comparison patterns and it always requires the definite article.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the comparison is parallel and correctly formed.
questions.context: A linguist examines parallel comparison structures.

options.text: This method is most reliable and more economical than the old one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Most reliable' is a superlative and cannot be part of a comparison with 'than'.

options.text: This method is more reliable and economical than the old one.
options.feedback: Wrong. Repeating 'more' before the second adjective is not wrong grammatically, but sharing it is the more economical parallel form here.

options.text: This method is more reliable and more economical than the old one.
options.feedback: Correct. Because both adjectives take 'more', the second can share it, and the comparison structure remains parallel.

options.text: This method is more reliable and most economical than the old one.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Most economical' is a superlative, which again cannot appear in a two-way comparison.

questions.explanation:
When several adjectives share the same comparative pattern, the auxiliary can be distributed across them, and examinations reward that parallelism.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly compares how two people performed.
questions.context: An exam item tests a comparison with a verb rather than an adjective.

options.text: She works as carefully more than he does.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'As carefully more' combines the equality and comparative patterns, which is not valid.

options.text: She works most carefully than he does.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Most carefully' is a superlative and cannot be followed by 'than'.

options.text: She works more careful than he does.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'More careful' uses the adjective form where the adverb is required to modify the verb 'works'.

options.text: She works more carefully than he does.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Carefully' is an adverb ending in -ly, so its comparative takes 'more' before it.

questions.explanation: Adverbs ending in -ly take more or most in the comparative and superlative, which is the opposite of the short adverbs.
